text: Pretraining in one screen Pretraining is self-supervised next-token prediction: a randomly initialised network reads trillions of tokens and is trained to maximise the log-likelihood of each token given the tokens before it.
label: core
key: predict every token from the tokens before it

text: Nobody labels anything; the text is its own answer key.
label: core
key: on text nobody labelled

text: It is the most expensive stage by far, and it sets the ceiling every later stage works under (the root page, Topic: llm-training-and-post-training , Axis 1, shows why reinforcement learning sharpens what pretraining put there rather than adding to it).
label: core
key: sets the ceiling every later stage works under

text: 1 · The objective Every variant below is trained with the same loss, cross-entropy over the vocabulary; they differ in what the model sees and which positions it must predict.
label: core
key: The alternatives use the same loss

text: Causal language modelling (the GPT lineage): predict every token from its prefix.
label: core
key: causal language modelling

text: The universal choice for generative LLMs, because every position of every sequence carries a training signal and the trained model generates by the same rule it was trained on.
label: core
key: Every position of every sequence carries a training signal

text: Masked language modelling (BERT): hide about 15% of tokens and predict them from both sides.
label: core
key: hides about 15% of tokens

text: Better for encoders (classification, retrieval), not for generation; the Seq vs Seq paper page trains matched encoder and decoder pairs and measures exactly this split.
label: core
key: trains matched encoders and decoders

text: Span corruption (T5): sample 15% of tokens, replace each contiguous run of them with a single sentinel token unique to that example, and train the decoder to emit only the dropped spans, each prefixed by its sentinel.
label: core
key: replaces each corrupted run with one sentinel

text: The difference from BERT's masked LM is the target: you predict the missing text rather than reconstruct the whole sequence, so decoder sequences stay short and a step is cheaper.
label: core
key: decoder sequences stay short and a step is cheap

text: UL2 (Unifying Language Learning, Tay et al.
label: core
key: Tay et al. 2022

text: 2022 ) generalised this into a mixture of denoisers, varying corruption rate and span length and prefixing each example with a mode token, so one model learns short-span denoising, long-span denoising and prefix LM at once.
label: core
key: mixes denoisers of different corruption rates

text: Mostly historical for LLMs now, but still the default when you pretrain an encoder-decoder; see the T5 paper page (18 min read, +4h 12m resources), which runs T5's own span-corruption code on any sentence, and Encoder-Decoder Gemma and T5Gemma 2 for the 2025 revival.
label: core
key: Encoder-Decoder Gemma and T5Gemma 2

text: Fill-in-the-middle (FIM) : cut a document into (prefix, middle, suffix) and move the middle to the end, so an ordinary causal model learns to infill.
label: core
key: moves the middle to the end

text: Standard for code models.
label: core
key: standard for code

text: 2022 found that training with a large FIM rate leaves left-to-right ability intact ("FIM for free"); DeepSeek-V3 applies FIM to 10% of documents in the prefix-suffix-middle order and reports no loss of next-token ability ( DeepSeek-V3, section 4.1 ).
label: core
key: FIM to 10% of documents in prefix-suffix-middle order

text: The per-512 counters are derived from the defaults: masked LM hides round(0.15 × 512) = 77; span corruption at mean span 3 makes round(77 / 3) = 26 spans, so the input is 512 − 77 + 26 + 1 = 462 tokens and the target 77 + 26 + 1 = 104 (T5's own code, run on the T5 paper page , does the same arithmetic).
label: core

text: How much the choice of objective is worth, measured T5 ran the comparison properly, holding architecture, data, compute and evaluation fixed and moving only the objective ( Raffel et al., section 3.3 ).
label: core
key: holding architecture, data, compute and evaluation fixed

text: The finding that matters is the shape of the result rather than the numbers: the gap between objective families is large (denoising beats prefix language modelling beats deshuffling), while the gap within the denoising family is close to nothing.
label: core
key: the gap within denoising is noise

text: BERT-style masking, MASS-style masking, sentinel replacement and outright token dropping all land within about two GLUE points of each other; corruption rates of 10%, 15% and 25% are indistinguishable and only 50% hurts; mean span lengths of 2, 3 and 5 are indistinguishable and 10 is slightly worse.
label: core
key: only a 50% rate and spans of 10 are worse

text: GLUE average on T5's validation sets, Tables 4 to 7 of the T5 paper , transcribed (so they match by construction); each panel is drawn on the same 72 to 86 scale.
label: core
key: each panel on the same 72 to 86 scale

text: The grey band is ±1 standard deviation of the baseline over 10 reruns (0.235, Table 1). derived ranges: families 82.96 − 73.17 = 9.79 points (about 42 standard deviations); corruption rates 10 to 25%: 83.28 − 82.82 = 0.46 (about 2); span lengths 2 to 5: 0.14.
label: core

text: The practical conclusion, and the reason this section is short rather than long: pick a denoising variant on computational cost, not on quality, and do not expect further tuning in this space to pay.
label: core
key: pick a denoising variant on cost, not quality

text: The same paper is also why the field's architecture default is worth knowing as a measured result and not a habit: at matched compute the encoder-decoder (83.28 GLUE) beat the decoder-only prefix LM (81.82), both trained with the denoising objective, and the field went decoder-only anyway, for reasons about in-context learning and serving cost that the comparison did not test ( Table 2 ).
label: core
key: encoder-decoder (83.28 GLUE) beat a decoder-only prefix LM (81.82)

text: Correction The old page quoted "a plain causal LM trails badly on understanding tasks, GLUE 74.70 against 83.28".
label: core
key: GLUE 74.70 against 83.28

text: In Table 2, 74.70 is a decoder-only language model trained with the denoising objective; the same decoder trained with the plain causal objective scored 73.78.
label: core
key: scored 73.78

text: Both trail the encoder-decoder's 83.28, so the point stands, but the 9-point gap is about the architecture (no bidirectional encoder), not the objective.
label: core
key: the 9-point gap is about the architecture

text: The objective comparison is Table 4: prefix LM 80.69 against BERT-style 82.96.
label: core
key: prefix LM 80.69 against BERT-style 82.96

text: 2 · Reading the loss L = −(1/T) Σ t log p θ (x t | x <t ) perplexity = e L L mean cross-entropy per token, in nats (divide by ln 2 for bits) T tokens in the evaluated text perplexity the effective number of equally likely choices per token Loss is reported as per-token cross-entropy or perplexity, and downstream ability tracks loss smoothly enough to make scaling laws work: a run's loss at a given size and token count can be forecast from small runs, and the Llama 3 paper forecast benchmark accuracy from it in two steps.
label: core
key: perplexity = e L

text: Three cautions make the number honest: Per-token loss depends on the tokenizer.
label: core
key: Per-token loss depends on the tokenizer

text: A tokenizer with longer tokens has fewer, harder tokens; compare models with different tokenizers in bits per byte (total bits over total bytes), not per token.
label: core
key: compare models with different tokenizers in bits per byte

text: The NanoGPT speedrun can use per-token loss (3.28) only because its rules fix the tokenizer and the validation stream ( modded-nanogpt rules ).
label: core
key: fix the tokenizer and the validation stream

text: The average hides the floor.
label: core
key: The average hides the floor

text: Some tokens are predictable (the rest of a word, the answer to a sum), others are genuine choices with an entropy no model can remove.
label: core
key: others are real choices whose entropy no model removes

text: The Anneal a toy tab shows this on a real run: the loss on the digits of an answer can fall to almost zero, while the loss on the operands of a random sum cannot go below about 3.25 bits per digit (the average of log 2 9 for a leading digit and log 2 10 for the second).
label: core
key: about 3.25 bits per digit

text: Held-out loss on high-quality text predicts downstream better than training loss , which moves with the data mix: when the mix changes at an anneal, training loss jumps or falls for reasons that have nothing to do with the model getting better.
label: core
key: Held-out loss on high-quality text predicts downstream better than training loss

text: 3 · Size against tokens Kaplan et al.
label: core
key: Kaplan et al. 2020

text: 2020 : loss follows power laws in model size N, dataset size D and compute C, and they concluded you should scale N faster than D.
label: core
key: size should grow faster than tokens

text: See the Scaling Laws paper page .
label: core
key: Kaplan et al. 2020

text: Chinchilla (Hoffmann et al.
label: core
key: Hoffmann et al. 2022

text: 2022) fixed Kaplan's learning-rate-schedule artefact (each of Kaplan's shorter runs was read off a cosine schedule planned for a longer one, so it was never annealed): compute-optimal training scales N and D equally, roughly D ≈ 20 tokens per parameter (1.4T / 70B = 20 derived ).
label: core
key: never annealed

text: Chinchilla (70B, 1.4T tokens) beat Gopher (280B) at equal compute.
label: core
key: Chinchilla beat it

text: See the Chinchilla paper page .
label: core
key: Chinchilla paper page

text: Post-Chinchilla practice : everyone deliberately "overtrains" far past compute-optimal because inference cost dominates the lifetime economics; a smaller model trained longer is cheaper to serve.
label: core
key: Why everyone over-trains

text: Llama 3 8B: about 15T tokens ( Llama 3.1 model card ) over 8B parameters is about 1,875 tokens per parameter derived (1,868 with the exact 8.03B).
label: core
key: 1,868 per parameter

text: What the allocation rules leave out : Chinchilla fixed the split between parameters and tokens but treated tokens as interchangeable, and that is the term doing the most work.
label: core
key: Tokens are not interchangeable

text: Decomposing progress from 2019 to 2025 attributes 3.24 times more compute-efficiency gain to data improvements than to model improvements (12.0 against 3.7 times at a 1e19-FLOP budget, 12.0 / 3.7 = 3.24 derived ), and finds the two largely independent ( Dwarkesh Patel and Jerry Han, September 2026 , 25 min).
label: core
key: 12.0 against 3.7 times

text: Taken with the rules above it reorders the priority list: allocation is solved, mixture is not, which is why the detail lives in Topic: data-curation-and-datasets and why the next section is the longest.
label: core
key: Allocation is largely solved; the mixture is not

text: Loss curves are also used prescriptively : fit a scaling law on small runs, then predict the big run's loss and pick hyperparameters. muP (μTransfer, Yang et al.
label: core
key: Scaling laws also set hyperparameters

text: 2022 ) parameterises the network so the best learning rate and initialisation found on a narrow model transfer to wider ones; used by many 2024+ labs unconfirmed as a count (labs rarely say), and visible in the speedrun's "zero-init projections (muP-like)".
label: core
key: zero-init projections (muP-like)

text: Go deeper: move a compute budget between Chinchilla's, Kaplan's and an over-trained allocation, with presets that show their residual against published runs, on the root page's Scaling calculator tab.
label: core

text: 4 · Data in stages Modern pretraining is multi-stage, not one homogeneous pass: Stage 1, bulk (about 90% of tokens or more) : filtered web (FineWeb- or DCLM-style), code, papers.
label: core
key: a bulk stage

text: OLMo 2's stage 1 was the OLMo 2 Mix: 3.90T tokens, 95.2% DCLM web pages, the rest StarCoder code, peS2o and arXiv papers, Wikipedia and two maths sets from Proof-Pile II ( OLMo 2, Tables 4 and 10 ).
label: core
key: 95.2% DCLM web pages

text: Mid-training, or the anneal : as the learning rate decays, up-weight high-quality data (curated maths, instruction-like text, synthetic data).
label: core
key: up-weights the best data

text: OLMo 2's Dolmino mix during the anneal gives outsized benchmark gains; Llama 3 does the same over its final 40M tokens ( Llama 3, section 3.4.3 ). "Annealing" means three different things in this literature (LR decay, this phase, and a cheap data experiment); the Optimisers page separates them.
label: core
key: final 40M tokens

text: Long-context extension : short-context pretraining for most tokens, then a final phase at 32K to 128K and beyond with upsampled long documents and RoPE rescaling.
label: core
key: long-context extension

text: SmolLM3 used 2 × 50B tokens (4K to 32K, then 64K); Llama 3 405B about 800B tokens in six steps from 8K to 128K.
label: core
key: about 800B tokens in six steps from 8K to 128K

label: core

text: OLMo 2 planned a cosine over 5T tokens and cut it at 3.90T, with the learning rate still at about 20% of peak derived (0.1 + 0.9 × ½(1 + cos(π × 3.90/5)) = 0.203), then spent 50B tokens, 1.3% of the run derived , decaying it linearly to zero on a different mix, three times over different data orders, and averaged the three ("souping").
label: core

text: SmolLM3 never decayed until the last 10%, and changed its mix twice.
label: core
key: held its learning rate flat until the last 10% and changed its mix twice

text: The SmolLM3 team chose its mixes by ablations on 3B models trained on 50B to 100B tokens ( SmolLM3 blog ); Llama 3 judges a new dataset by annealing a half-trained 8B linearly to zero over 40B tokens with 30% of the data from the candidate ( section 3.1.3 ), a cheap experiment instead of a scaling-law study.
label: core
key: 30% of the data from the candidate

text: Key idea: the data mixture is now the main open lever; the architecture is largely converged (pre-norm decoder, RMSNorm, SwiGLU, RoPE, grouped-query attention; mixture-of-experts for the compute-rich).
label: core
key: largely converged

text: The LLM Architecture Gallery shows the convergence model by model.
label: core

text: 5 · What the anneal buys An anneal pulls two levers at once: the learning rate falls to zero, and the data switches to the best you have.
label: core
key: An anneal pulls two levers at once

text: Any claim that "annealing gave +X" is a compound of the two unless an ablation separated them.
label: core
key: is a compound of the two unless an ablation separated them

text: OLMo 2 ran exactly that ablation on its 7B: from the checkpoint at 4T tokens, 50B tokens with the learning rate decayed to zero on the unchanged pretraining mix, against the same schedule on high-quality mixes ( Table 11 ).
label: core
key: from the checkpoint at 4T tokens

text: Predict: on the maths dev set (GSM*, 200 GSM8K questions), how much of the anneal's gain comes from the learning-rate decay alone?
label: core
key: 200 GSM8K questions

text: Most of it About half None of it 4T checkpoint, no anneal + LR to zero, same mix + high-quality mix (web, maths, instructions) OLMo 2 Table 11: "n/a (pretrain checkpoint)", "PT Mix" and "Web FT7 FW2 + Math + Ins" rows, each 50B tokens from the same 4T checkpoint. derived splits: LR part = PT Mix − checkpoint; data part = new mix − PT Mix.
label: core
key: Web FT7 FW2 + Math + Ins

text: The bars reproduce Table 11 by construction (transcribed).
label: core
key: reproduce Table 11 by construction

text: GSM* is 200 questions, so one score has a binomial standard error of about 3.2 to 3.5 points and a difference about 4.5 to 4.7 (√(p(1−p)/200)); the multiple-choice scores average many more questions and are tighter, but the paper gives no error bars for them.
label: core
key: about 4.5 to 4.7

text: The answer is the most useful single fact about anneals: on knowledge and multiple-choice tasks most of the gain is the learning-rate decay (OLMES +4.4 of +6.1, MMLU +2.0 of +3.3), while on maths all of it is the data (decay alone −1.5, within noise; the new mix +19.5).
label: core
key: OLMES +4.4 of +6.1, MMLU +2.0 of +3.3

text: The shipped OLMo 2 7B, with three souped 50B anneals on the final Dolmino mix, went from 24.1 to 67.5 on full GSM8K and 59.8 to 63.7 on MMLU, +10.6 points on average ( Table 9 ).

text: 7 · Running it well Batch size.
label: core
key: Batch size.

text: Use the critical batch size heuristic: below it, a larger batch buys nearly proportional speed; above it, it wastes compute, and it grows as the loss falls ( McCandlish et al.
label: core
key: Below the critical batch size

text: 2018 ; Kaplan's form is plotted on the Scaling Laws page ).
label: core
key: Kaplan's form is plotted on the Scaling Laws page

text: So ramp it rather than fix it: GPT-3 ramped linearly from 32K tokens to the full batch over the first 4 to 12B tokens ( GPT-3, Appendix B ); Llama 3 405B went from 4M to 8M tokens after 252M tokens and to 16M after 2.87T ( section 3.4.1 ); the speedrun's record 46 was a batch-size schedule.
label: core
key: to 16M after 2.87T

text: Warmup plus cosine is classic; WSD (warmup-stable-decay) is now popular because you can branch anneals off the stable plateau without committing to a total token count, which is how SmolLM3 above was run.
label: core
key: anneals can branch off the plateau without committing to a token count

text: The full family comparison (shapes, cooldown length and curve, decay-free options like schedule-free and WSM) lives on Optimisers and learning-rate schedulers ; the WSM paper page trains the decay-free option.
label: core
key: Optimisers and learning-rate schedulers

text: Stability. z-loss or logit soft-capping, QK-norm (OLMo 2 moved to QK-norm plus reordered norms specifically for stability; its ablations are replayed on the OLMo 2 paper page ), bf16 with fp32 master weights, gradient clipping at 1.0 (GPT-3, OLMo 2, SmolLM3 and the toy on this page all clip at 1.0), and watch for loss spikes correlated with bad data shards.
label: core
key: OLMo 2 moved to QK-norm plus reordered norms

text: Llama 3 lowered its early batch size for stability and reports few spikes and no interventions.
label: core
key: few spikes and no interventions

label: core

label: core

text: Common mistakes "The anneal added 18 points on maths, so annealing is the trick" Two levers moved.
